evidence.claim: The president serves a five-year term with only one reelection, is supreme commander of the armed forces, may declare war/make peace and conclude treaties with DPR approval, appoints and dismisses ministers, and can be removed only through the constitutional impeachment process.
evidence.title: The 1945 Constitution of the Republic of Indonesia, Indonesia
evidence.excerpt: The president serves a five-year term with only one reelection, is supreme commander of the armed forces, may declare war/make peace and conclude treaties with DPR approval, appoints and dismisses ministers, and can be removed only through the constitutional impeachment process.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official constitutional text on an authoritative legal database; stable and directly governing 2022 office powers.
evidence.period_fit: Standing constitutional framework in force throughout 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Office-level authority and constraints for Jokowi as president; not a performance claim.
contrary_evidence: No nuclear-specific authority appears in the text; it defines general executive powers, not nuclear command.
Several core powers are constrained by DPR and judicial procedures.

evidence.claim: Jokowi said the constitution already regulates presidential terms and that everyone must obey it, in response to three-term talk.
evidence.title: Soal Presiden Tiga Periode, Presiden Jokowi: Kita Harus Taat Konstitusi
evidence.excerpt: Jokowi said the constitution already regulates presidential terms and that everyone must obey it, in response to three-term talk.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct presidential statement published by the Cabinet Secretariat on the same day.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 ruler statement during the term-extension controversy.
contrary_evidence: Self-reporting is not independent verification of broader coalition behavior.
It rejects three-term talk but does not by itself show long-term institutional restraint.

evidence.claim: Jokowi said the 2024 election schedule was already fixed and that the government should prevent speculation about postponing the election or extending the president’s term.
evidence.title: Introductory Remarks of President of the Republic of Indonesia at Limited Cabinet Meeting on the Preparation for the 2024 Simultaneous General Elections and Regional Elections
evidence.excerpt: Jokowi said the 2024 election schedule was already fixed and that the government should prevent speculation about postponing the election or extending the president’s term.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct presidential remarks published by the Cabinet Secretariat with explicit dates and policy context.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 statement during the term-extension debate.
contrary_evidence: This addresses constitutional timing, not nuclear or existential-risk policy.
It shows rejection of postponement speculation, not a broader institutional reform program.

evidence.claim: Jokowi ordered his cabinet to stop discussing election delay or extension of the presidential term and said the election delay/extension idea should stop.
evidence.title: Indonesia president seeks to end talk he is angling for a new term
evidence.excerpt: Jokowi ordered his cabinet to stop discussing election delay or extension of the presidential term and said the election delay/extension idea should stop.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous Reuters reporting with explicit ruler quotation and constitutional context.
evidence.period_fit: Direct April 2022 conduct in the target year.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Jokowi statement and cabinet instruction.
contrary_evidence: Reuters notes critics still saw the response as ambiguous rather than an unqualified rejection.
The article also shows the extension idea had already gained momentum among political figures, so this is partly reactive.

evidence.claim: Indonesia remained partly free, the electoral framework was largely democratic but had problematic provisions, and the country continued to have significant pluralism with multiple peaceful transfers of power while facing military influence, online propaganda, and limits on political equality.
evidence.title: Indonesia: Freedom in the World 2022 Country Report
evidence.excerpt: Indonesia remained partly free, the electoral framework was largely democratic but had problematic provisions, and the country continued to have significant pluralism with multiple peaceful transfers of power while facing military influence, online propaganda, and limits on political equality.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Major annual democracy assessment with detailed country coding and narrative explanation.
evidence.period_fit: Standing 2022 country baseline, not a single event.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly inherited/system-level context; some cabinet military appointments are attributed to Jokowi in the report, but most findings are structural.
contrary_evidence: Much of the content reflects inherited institutions and system-level constraints rather than 2022 presidential choice.
The report is a synthesis, not a direct account of Jokowi's intent.

evidence.claim: Internet access in Papua was disrupted again in 2022, critics and journalists faced criminal charges and harassment for online activity, protesters in Wadas experienced connectivity restrictions and arrests, and the government was suspected of spyware use and later platform-blocking efforts.
evidence.title: Indonesia: Freedom on the Net 2022 Country Report
evidence.excerpt: Internet access in Papua was disrupted again in 2022, critics and journalists faced criminal charges and harassment for online activity, protesters in Wadas experienced connectivity restrictions and arrests, and the government was suspected of spyware use and later platform-blocking efforts.
evidence.source_locator: overview lines 85-86; key developments lines 89-94; A1 lines 106-107; B4 lines 285-286; lines 142-143
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Detailed annual digital-rights assessment with multiple 2022 incidents and direct country coding.
evidence.period_fit: Target-year digital freedom and administrative control evidence.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly state-level attribution under Jokowi's administration; not all incidents are shown to be directly ordered by Jokowi personally.
contrary_evidence: Some disruptions are described as infrastructural or unacknowledged, so causation is not always direct.
The report also notes Indonesia retains substantial media pluralism, so this is not a closed-system case.

evidence.claim: Indonesia had a diverse media environment, but electronic-communications laws threatened digital-media independence, authorities still used defamation charges, the ITE law contained vague offences that applied to social media, and many politicians used paid commenters or 'buzzers' to shape opinion.
evidence.title: Indonesia
evidence.publisher: Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, University of Oxford
evidence.excerpt: Indonesia had a diverse media environment, but electronic-communications laws threatened digital-media independence, authorities still used defamation charges, the ITE law contained vague offences that applied to social media, and many politicians used paid commenters or 'buzzers' to shape opinion.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Academic annual country report with explicit explanation of the legal and media environment.
evidence.ruler_attribution: System-level media environment under Jokowi's administration; not a single presidential order.
contrary_evidence: The report also says the media environment remained diverse and no longer primarily censored by government.
This is background context, not proof of direct 2022 presidential censorship.

evidence.claim: CPJ said a recent rash of harassment and intimidation showed press freedom under assault in Indonesia and urged Jokowi's government to protect and uphold media freedoms.
evidence.title: Indonesian journalists face wave of harassment and intimidation
evidence.excerpt: CPJ said a recent rash of harassment and intimidation showed press freedom under assault in Indonesia and urged Jokowi's government to protect and uphold media freedoms.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous press-freedom monitoring with explicit appeal to the Jokowi ప్రభుత్వం.
evidence.period_fit: Target-year press freedom and intimidation evidence.
evidence.ruler_attribution: State responsibility is attributed to Jokowi's government, but the page does not identify a direct presidential order.
contrary_evidence: This is an advocacy/monitoring source and does not itself establish command responsibility for each incident.
It describes a wave of incidents rather than a single systemic decree.

evidence.claim: The government restricted speech through defamation, hate-speech, blasphemy, and false-information penalties; there were numerous reports of law being used to limit criticism of the government; and the updated criminal code criminalized insulting state institutions and criticizing the president and vice president.
evidence.title: 2022 Country Report on Human Rights Practices: Indonesia
evidence.excerpt: The government restricted speech through defamation, hate-speech, blasphemy, and false-information penalties; there were numerous reports of law being used to limit criticism of the government; and the updated criminal code criminalized insulting state institutions and criticizing the president and vice president.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Government human-rights report summarizing 2022 conditions with legal specificity.
evidence.ruler_attribution: State-level, under Jokowi's administration; the report does not isolate Jokowi as the direct author of each restriction.
contrary_evidence: The report also says the constitution provides freedom of expression and that the code was not yet in force by year-end.
This is a broad rights report rather than a direct act by Jokowi.

evidence.claim: HRW said the 2022 criminal code seriously violated human rights and undermined freedom of speech and association; it also noted that Jokowi had previously delayed an earlier draft after mass protests and later ordered cabinet 'socialization' of the bill.
evidence.title: Indonesia: New Criminal Code Disastrous for Rights
evidence.excerpt: HRW said the 2022 criminal code seriously violated human rights and undermined freedom of speech and association; it also noted that Jokowi had previously delayed an earlier draft after mass protests and later ordered cabinet 'socialization' of the bill.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Major rights organization with explicit 2022 legal analysis and historical comparison.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 legislative outcome and a prior ruler response used as comparison.
evidence.ruler_attribution: The passage of the law is a parliamentary act under Jokowi's administration; the earlier delay is directly attributed to Jokowi.
contrary_evidence: The report shows Jokowi had previously responded to protest pressure by delaying an earlier draft, which is a mitigating fact.
The final law was passed by parliament, so the immediate act is not uniquely a presidential decision.

evidence.claim: The new criminal code criminalized insulting the president and vice president, insulting state institutions, blasphemy expansions, and sex outside marriage, with complaints required for some offenses and a three-year implementation window before it takes effect.
evidence.title: Indonesia: New Criminal Code Passed by Parliament
evidence.excerpt: The new criminal code criminalized insulting the president and vice president, insulting state institutions, blasphemy expansions, and sex outside marriage, with complaints required for some offenses and a three-year implementation window before it takes effect.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Government legal bulletin with precise statutory summary and enactment date.
evidence.period_fit: Direct late-2022 legal change in the target year.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Parliamentary enactment under Jokowi's presidency; not a personal order by Jokowi in the text itself.
contrary_evidence: The article says opponents can seek judicial review and that the law was not yet in force at year-end.
The piece summarizes legal text rather than enforcement outcomes.

evidence.claim: RSF said Jokowi did not keep his promises about press freedom, the military blocked coverage of force in Papua, and journalists still had to contend with blasphemy and ITE-law risks.
evidence.title: Indonésie 2022 - EN
evidence.excerpt: RSF said Jokowi did not keep his promises about press freedom, the military blocked coverage of force in Papua, and journalists still had to contend with blasphemy and ITE-law risks.
evidence.source_locator: political context and legal framework lines 317-322
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Annual RSF country analysis with explicit Jokowi attribution and legal-framework detail.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mixed: direct criticism of Jokowi's record, but much of the restriction is institutional and military rather than personally ordered.
contrary_evidence: The same page notes the 1999 press law created an independent press council and that the media landscape remained diverse.
This is a regional analysis, not a single 2022 incident report.
